title: Signal-fused admission controller with kernel-adaptive windowing
creator: Maya Chen
description: Problem: Persistent 95th/99th tail latency regressions for mixed short/long sequence workloads due to suboptimal admission signals and aggressive kernel switching during prefill/decoding transitions. Goal: Replace the current thresholded prefill admission with a signal-fusion controller that aggregates early runtime hints (sequence-length priors, kv-cache hit estimates, model-kernel cost deltas, and recent per-GPU congestion) to compute a short-time admission window size and kernel-advice token budget. The controller should: 1) stabilize batch shaping across bursty traffic, 2) avoid mid-prefill kernel swaps that cause stalls, and 3) gracefully degrade throughput under constrained capacity while protecting latency SLOs.
acceptance_criteria: 1) 95th percentile latency for mixed short/long (10%-90% split) workloads improves by >= 20% vs baseline under identical load traces; 2) No increased error/timeout rate at 99.9% confidence; 3) Kernel change frequency per request reduced by >= 60% for requests that include both prefill and decode stages; 4) Feature flag rollout runs successfully on staging fleet and can be toggled per-tenant.
design_notes: Controller inputs: admission queue depth, recent per-GPU decode latency distribution, predicted end-of-prefill token count (from prompt classifier), kv-cache hit probability, model->kernel cost table. Decision outputs: admit_count (tokens), preferred_kernel_hint, degrade_mode (batch smaller / fall back to safe-kernel). We will implement a lightweight runtime estimator that samples kernel runtimes for canonical length buckets and caches a sliding-window cost table. The admission decision uses a weighted-sum heuristic (configurable weights), with a short-horizon PID-like dampener to avoid oscillation. Important: keep execution path very small (O(1) per incoming request) to avoid adding scheduler overhead.
tradeoffs_and_risks:
- More accurate signals require telemetry and sampling; cost of sampling must be bounded to avoid additional noise.
- Heuristic vs learned policy: we start with deterministic fusion rules to ship quickly; a learned policy (RL or bandit) is planned as follow-up but introduces training/metric drift risk.
- Tenant isolation: misestimated kernels could favor throughput for some tenants; mitigate via per-tenant override and safe-fallback kernel.
- Complexity: introduce a centralized decision appears simpler but limits horizontal scalability; prefer local per-GPU lightweight controller with periodic cluster syncs.
rollout_plan: Phase 0: Integration tests + synthetic trace bench (local) - target pass by 2026-03-20. Phase 1: Canary on 5% of staging fleet with feature flag (runtime-1.24-canary) for 72h and continuous perf/quality checks. Phase 2: Gradual ramp to 25% and then 100% for non-critical tenants. Phase 3: Expose tenant-level opt-in and force-off for Dedicated customers. If any safety guard trips (SLO breach, error increase), rollback via flag within 5 minutes.
monitoring_and_alerting: Dashboards: per-route 50/95/99 latency, kernel-change-per-request, admitted_batch_size distribution, per-GPU QPS and queue length. Alerts: 95th latency increase > 15% over baseline for > 10m; kernel-change rate spike > 2x baseline; tail error rate increase of 0.1%. All alerts should include link to rollback toggle and recent logs sample.
testing_strategy: Unit tests for decision heuristics, integration tests with fake kernel cost table, end-to-end bench using replayed production traces (short/long mixes), and fault-injection test where sampled kernel runtimes are perturbed. Add regression tests to CI that validate kernel change frequency does not increase for canonical traces.
